title: Job Roles & the Production Workflow
description: Discover who does what in media production and how projects move from idea to finished product.
content_html:
Who Makes Media?

Creating a media product — whether a film, a website or a video game — is rarely the work of one person. It requires a team of specialists, each responsible for a different aspect of the project. Understanding the key job roles in media production, and the order in which their work happens, is essential both for the exam and for any practical media work you carry out.

Creative and Management Roles

At the top of a production, the producer manages the budget, schedule and overall delivery of a project. They are responsible for making sure the product is finished on time, within budget and to the client's specification. The director makes the creative decisions: visual style, tone, performances and storytelling choices in film and TV productions. In advertising and corporate media, an art director or creative director plays an equivalent role. The graphic designer creates visual assets — logos, layouts, typography and imagery — for print, digital and moving-image products. An animator brings static images or 3D models to life using specialist software such as Adobe After Effects or Autodesk Maya.

Key Fact

Key media job roles include: producer (budget and schedule), director (creative decisions), editor (post-production assembly), graphic designer (visual assets), animator (motion and animation), photographer (stills), web developer (websites and apps), games designer (game rules and experience), and copywriter (written content). Each role has a distinct function in the production process.

Technical and Specialist Roles

The editor assembles raw footage, audio and graphics into the finished product — in film and video they work in editing software such as Adobe Premiere Pro or Final Cut Pro; in publishing they use InDesign to lay out pages. A photographer captures still images for use across print, digital and advertising products. A web developer writes the code that brings a website or app to life, using languages such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A games designer defines the rules, levels, mechanics and player experience of a video game; they work with artists and programmers to translate their vision into a playable product. A copywriter produces all the written text in a media product — advertising straplines, website copy, script dialogue or magazine articles.

This is one of the most commonly confused pairs in the exam. The producer oversees the logistical and financial side of a production: they set the budget, manage the schedule, hire the crew and ensure the project is delivered to the client. The director is responsible for the creative vision: how the product looks, sounds and feels. On a small production, one person might do both jobs, but they remain conceptually distinct. A useful memory hook is: the producer handles the money and the meetings; the director handles the camera and the performances.

The Three Phases of the Production Workflow

All media production — regardless of sector — follows a three-phase production workflow: pre-production, production and post-production. This framework helps teams plan their work, manage resources and deliver a finished product that meets the client's requirements.

Pre-Production, Production and Post-Production

Pre-production covers everything that happens before any content is actually created: writing the script or brief, storyboarding, casting, scouting locations, creating mood boards, planning schedules and budgets, and sourcing assets such as images or music. Production is the active creation phase — filming takes place, photographs are shot, web pages are coded, or game levels are built. Post-production begins once raw content has been gathered: footage is edited, audio is mixed, colour grading is applied, graphics are added, and the product is reviewed and refined before final delivery.

Key Fact

Pre-production (planning): scripts, storyboards, mood boards, schedules, budgets, location scouting. Production (creating): filming, photographing, coding, building. Post-production (finishing): editing, audio mixing, colour grading, graphic overlays, review and final delivery.

Students often write that post-production only means "editing the video". In reality, post-production encompasses a wide range of processes: audio mixing and sound design, music licensing and composition, visual effects (VFX) and colour grading, the creation and integration of motion graphics or animated titles, quality assurance review, and final export or delivery to the client or distributor. In an exam, naming several distinct post-production tasks — not just "editing" — will score significantly higher on explain and describe questions.
exam_tip_html: When describing a job role, always state clearly what that person does, not just their job title. Examiners want to see understanding: writing "the editor assembles footage, applies colour grading and adds music to create the final cut" scores more than "the editor edits the video". For questions about the production workflow, name the phase and then give at least two specific tasks from that phase — this is especially important for "describe" and "explain" questions worth 3 or more marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Key media job roles include producer (budget and schedule), director (creative decisions), editor (assembly and finishing), graphic designer (visual assets), animator, photographer, web developer, games designer and copywriter — each with a distinct function.
  • All media production follows three phases: pre-production (planning and preparation), production (active creation) and post-production (editing, mixing, review and delivery).
  • The producer manages logistics and budget while the director makes creative decisions — these are separate roles even when one person carries out both.

glossary_terms.definition: Specific functions carried out by individuals within a media production team, each contributing distinct skills to the finished product.
The structured sequence of stages that a media production passes through, from initial planning to final delivery.
The planning stage of a media project, where ideas are developed, resources are organised and all preparation work is completed before any content is created.
The finishing stage of a media project, where raw content is edited, audio is mixed, graphics are added and the product is reviewed before final delivery.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a responsibility of the producer on a media production?
A) Making creative decisions about visual style
B) Writing the script and dialogue
C) Managing the budget and schedule
D) Editing the footage in post-production
practice_questions.marks: C) Managing the budget and schedule [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two tasks that take place during the pre-production phase of a media project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: writing a script [1]; creating a storyboard [1]; creating a mood board [1]; planning a schedule or timeline [1]; setting a budget [1]; scouting or selecting locations [1]; sourcing assets (images, music, fonts) [1]. Answers that merely describe production tasks (e.g. filming) score zero. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of a graphic designer differs from the role of an animator.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a graphic designer creates still images'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a graphic designer creates static visual assets such as logos, layouts and typography for print or digital use, whereas an animator uses specialist software to create moving images or motion graphics'). A fully developed answer with an applied example scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for instance, on a film poster campaign, the graphic designer would create the poster layout and typography, while an animator would produce the title sequence motion graphics for the trailer'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the post-production phase of a film production. Give one example of a specific task carried out at this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): post-production is the stage after filming is complete, where raw footage is assembled into the finished product through editing; it also includes audio mixing, sound design, adding visual effects and motion graphics, colour grading and quality review before final delivery (2 marks for a developed description covering multiple processes; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'the footage is edited').
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a colourist adjusts the colour and contrast of each shot in software such as DaVinci Resolve so all scenes look visually consistent, even if they were filmed on different days or in different lighting conditions (2 marks for a specific, developed example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A small media company has been asked to produce a 3-minute promotional video for a local charity. The team consists of a producer, a director, a videographer and an editor.

Discuss how each job role contributes to the successful completion of this project across the three phases of production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion that links specific job roles to specific tasks within at least two of the three phases, applied to the charity video scenario. For example: the producer sets the schedule and manages the charity client relationship throughout all phases; the director shapes the visual approach in pre-production (concept, storyboard) and directs filming during production; the editor assembles and grades the footage in post-production. Contrast or complexity should be present, e.g. noting that on a small team these roles may overlap, creating scheduling tension.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two roles described with tasks across phases, with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One role or one phase described with limited detail.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague statement about the team with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student argues that pre-production is the most important phase of the production workflow because it determines the success of everything that follows.

Evaluate the extent to which thorough pre-production planning leads to a higher-quality finished media product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues thorough pre-production is crucial because it identifies problems early, aligns the team around a shared creative vision, and ensures resources (locations, assets, budget) are secured before expensive production begins; then challenges this with the counter-argument that even outstanding planning cannot fully account for creative decisions made during production (a director may change approach when filming) or post-production discoveries (unexpected footage may produce a better edit). A substantiated judgement is reached about the relationship between planning and quality, going beyond a simple list.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two well-developed points on each side with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on the value of pre-production with limited counter-argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic statement about planning with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which job role is responsible for managing the budget and schedule on a media production?
Which job role uses software such as Adobe Premiere Pro or Final Cut Pro to assemble footage into the finished product?
Creating a storyboard and scouting locations are tasks that happen during the _____ phase of production.
A _____ writes the code that brings a website or app to life, using languages such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Match each phase of production to the tasks that happen within it.
right: Editing, audio mixing and colour grading

flashcard_questions.q: What is the producer's main responsibility on a media production?
flashcard_questions.a: The producer is responsible for managing the budget, schedule and overall delivery of the project to the client.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the director control on a film or TV production?
flashcard_questions.a: The director controls the creative decisions, shaping the visual style, tone and storytelling approach of the production.
An editor assembles raw footage, audio and graphics into the finished product using editing software such as Premiere Pro.

flashcard_questions.q: Which job role creates logos, layouts and typography for print and digital products?

flashcard_questions.a: Brings static images or 3D models to life using motion and specialist software.
Written text for media products, such as scripts, advertising slogans or web copy.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three phases of the production workflow in order?
Name two tasks that happen in pre-production.
flashcard_questions.a: Scripting and storyboarding (also accept mood boarding, budgeting, scheduling, location scouting).

flashcard_questions.q: What takes place during the production phase?
flashcard_questions.a: The active creation of content: filming, coding, photographing or building game levels.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two processes that happen in post-production beyond basic editing.
flashcard_questions.a: Audio mixing and colour grading (also accept adding graphics, visual effects, quality review).

flashcard_questions.q: What does a games designer do?
flashcard_questions.a: A games designer defines the rules, mechanics, levels and overall player experience of a video game, working with artists and programmers.

flashcard_questions.q: What programming languages does a web developer typically use?
flashcard_questions.a: A web developer typically uses HTML to structure content, CSS to style it, and JavaScript to add interactive behaviour.

hero_image_caption: From the producer's schedule to the editor's timeline, media production is a collaborative process built around clearly defined job roles and a structured three-phase workflow.
